claim: Ebola virus disease first emerged in 1976 in Zaire (now the Democratic Republic of the Congo).
source: Following the initial emergence in 1976 in Zaire (now the Democratic Republic of the Congo [DRC]) (Report of an International Commission, 1978)
evidence: Supported by citation to Report of an International Commission, 1978

claim: Epidemics of Ebola virus disease have occurred, on average, every 12–24 months.
source: epidemics of Ebola virus disease (EVD) have occurred, on average, every 12–24 months (Rosello et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Rosello et al., 2015

claim: Ebola virus disease is caused by the Ebola Zaire virus.
source: EVD is a viral haemorrhagic fever first caused by the Ebola Zaire virus (EZV)
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about EVD etiology

claim: The case fatality rate of Ebola virus disease is 25–90%.
source: with a case fatality rate of 25–90% (In press, 2023b)
evidence: Supported by citation to In press, 2023b

claim: A major Ebola outbreak in the northeastern provinces of DRC between 2018 and 2020 resulted in over 3300 reported cases.
source: A major outbreak in the northeastern provinces of DRC between 2018 and 2020 resulted in over 3300 reported cases and over 2100 deaths (WHO Regional Office for Africa, 2020; Figure 1)
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO Regional Office for Africa, 2020 and reference to Figure 1

claim: The 2018-2020 DRC Ebola outbreak resulted in over 2100 deaths.
source: A major outbreak in the northeastern provinces of DRC between 2018 and 2020 resulted in over 3300 reported cases and over 2100 deaths (WHO Regional Office for Africa, 2020; Figure 1)
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO Regional Office for Africa, 2020 and reference to Figure 1

claim: Transmission of Ebola Zaire virus occurs mainly through direct contact during the symptomatic phase of infection.
source: Transmission of EZV occurs mainly through direct contact during the symptomatic phase of infection
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about Ebola transmission

claim: Isolation of infected individuals with strict infection control, contact tracing, and safe burials has been key to controlling past EVD outbreaks.
source: isolation of infected individuals with strict infection control, contact tracing, and safe burials has been key to controlling past EVD outbreaks (Kucharski et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kucharski et al., 2015

claim: Setting specific challenges can hamper Ebola containment efforts.
source: although setting specific challenges can hamper containment efforts (Adongo et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Adongo et al., 2016

claim: Two Ebola vaccines are now licensed for use.
source: with two vaccines now licensed for use (In press, 2023a; Woolsey and Geisbert, 2021)
evidence: Supported by citations to In press, 2023a and Woolsey and Geisbert, 2021

claim: EVD outbreaks typically occur in resource-poor settings where limited communication and poor accessibility make logistics of surveillance and vaccination campaigns challenging.
source: EVD outbreaks typically occur in resource-poor settings where limited communication and poor accessibility make logistics of surveillance and vaccination campaigns challenging.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about EVD outbreak contexts

claim: Mathematical and statistical models have been used extensively to forecast the spread of infectious diseases, including EVD.
source: Mathematical and statistical models have been used extensively to forecast the spread of infectious diseases, including EVD (Chowell et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Chowell et al., 2017

claim: Violent conflicts or flooding can seriously hinder, interrupt, or even reverse the impact of Ebola containment efforts.
source: For example, violent conflicts or flooding can seriously hinder, interrupt, or even reverse the impact of containment efforts (Adongo et al., 2016; Wannier et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to Adongo et al., 2016 and Wannier et al., 2019

claim: Changes in healthcare capacity and health-seeking behaviour of patients can strengthen or weaken efforts to reduce Ebola transmission.
source: Moreover, changes in healthcare capacity and health-seeking behaviour of patients can strengthen or weaken efforts to reduce transmission (Funk et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Funk et al., 2017

claim: The timing and impact of contextual factors affecting Ebola outbreaks are notoriously difficult to predict using mathematical models.
source: The timing and impact of these factors are notoriously difficult to predict using mathematical models.
evidence: Based on inference from the discussion of challenges in modeling contextual factors

claim: A study evaluated short-term forecasts and season-wide predictions of reports of influenza-like illness in the United States and found that humans tended to perform better than mathematical and statistical models.
source: The first of these evaluated short-term forecasts and season-wide predictions of reports of influenza-like illness in the United States (Farrow et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Farrow et al., 2017

claim: Two studies compared short-term forecasts of COVID-19 cases and deaths in Germany, Poland, and the United Kingdom, finding that humans tended to perform better than models when predicting cases.
source: two studies (Bosse et al., 2022; Bosse et al., 2023) compared short-term forecasts of cases of and deaths from COVID-19, firstly in Germany and Poland and secondly in the United Kingdom. All three studies found that humans tended to perform better than the mathematical and statistical models selected for comparison when predicting cases.
evidence: Supported by citations to Bosse et al., 2022 and Bosse et al., 2023

claim: COVID-focused studies found that human ensembles performed worse than the ensemble prediction of models when predicting deaths.
source: However, the COVID-focused studies found that the human ensembles performed worse than the ensemble prediction of the models when predicting deaths.
evidence: Supported by reference to COVID-focused studies (Bosse et al., 2022; Bosse et al., 2023)

claim: A study conducted early in the COVID-19 pandemic found that both experts and laypeople typically underpredicted the impact overall, but experts' forecasts were more accurate and better calibrated than laypeople.
source: A study conducted early in the COVID-19 pandemic (Recchia et al., 2021) evaluated the relative ability of laypeople and experts to predict the course of the UK epidemic over the first calendar year. The study found that both experts and laypeople typically underpredicted the impact overall; however, experts' forecasts were more accurate and better calibrated than laypeople.
evidence: Supported by citation to Recchia et al., 2021

claim: A study of expert predictions in the United States found that the ensemble outperformed every expert individually over the first year of COVID-19.
source: A study of expert predictions in the United States (McAndrew and Reich, 2022) evaluated their weekly forecasts of case incidence and total deaths in the first year against a pooled ensemble of all predictions. The study found that the ensemble outperformed every expert individually over the period of the study.
evidence: Supported by citation to McAndrew and Reich, 2022

claim: Experts in EVD epidemiology with knowledge of the local geography speaking English or French were identified by convenience sampling and snowball sampling.
source: Experts in EVD epidemiology with knowledge of the local geography speaking English or French were identified originally by convenience sampling. The pool of experts was then expanded through recommendation from the identified experts (snowball sampling).

claim: A pilot study was carried out in November 2019.
source: A pilot study was carried out in November 2019.

claim: Monthly interviews were held over WhatsApp in December 2019, January 2020, February 2020, and March 2020.
source: Subsequently, monthly interviews were held over WhatsApp in December 2019, January 2020, February 2020, and March 2020.

claim: Experts were provided with an interactive map of the outbreak area showing the number of total cases during the outbreak and during the two preceding weeks.
source: Experts were also provided with an interactive map of the outbreak area and surrounding HZs showing the number of total cases during the outbreak and during the two preceding weeks for reference (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Description of the study methodology with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Experts were asked to estimate the number of reported probable and confirmed cases per health zone during the following month using the online MATCH Uncertainty Elicitation Tool.
source: Experts were asked to estimate the number of reported probable and confirmed cases they would expect per HZ during the following month using the online MATCH Uncertainty Elicitation Tool (Morris et al., 2014; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Description of the study methodology with citation to Morris et al., 2014

claim: The 'roulette' (chips and bins) method was used for expert elicitation, where experts placed 20 chips over available bins representing 5% probability each.
source: The 'roulette' (chips and bins) method was used. Experts were instructed to place a total of 20 chips over the available bins (0–1 cases, 2–4 cases, …, 48–50 cases). Therefore, each chip represented for the expert a 5% probability that the number of cases was in the bin where the chip was placed.

claim: The modelling framework included an autoregressive component and a spatial component.
source: The model was formed of two components, the autoregressive component and the spatial component.

claim: Two spatial kernels were used: a gravity model and an adjacency-based model.
source: We used two spatial kernels, both of which use proximity of HZs to each other and their respective population size

claim: The model was fitted to historical data from the 60 days prior to the date the forecast was made.
source: To forecast cases, we fitted the spatiotemporal model to historical data from the 60 days prior to the date the forecast was made

claim: The model was fitted using the No U-Turn Sampling (NUTS) method for Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with Stan.
source: We fit the model using the No U-Turn Sampling (NUTS) method for Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with Stan (Stan Team, 2012), a probabilistic programming framework.
evidence: Description of the modeling methodology with citation to Stan Team, 2012

claim: 1000 iterations were performed for each forecast date.
source: We performed 1000 iterations for each forecast date.

claim: Forecasts were evaluated using the Brier score.
source: We evaluated the forecasts using the Brier score, a proper scoring rule which quantifies how accurate a forecast or a group of forecasts is when compared to true data after the event.

claim: Over the study period, 40 interviews were conducted with 15 experts.
source: Over the study period, we conducted a total of 40 interviews with 15 experts, 3 of which took place during the pilot phase (November 2019).

claim: Eight experts worked at the World Health Organization.
source: Eight experts worked at the World Health Organization

claim: Four experts worked at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine.
source: four at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine

claim: Two experts worked for Médecins Sans Frontières.
source: two for Médecins Sans Frontières

claim: One expert worked at the DRC Ministry of Health.
source: and one at the DRC Ministry of Health

claim: Most experts (10/15) had more than 5 years of experience working in infectious disease epidemiology.
source: Most experts (10/15) had more than 5 years of experience working in infectious disease epidemiology.

claim: About half of the interviews (21 of 40) were conducted with experts who were in the outbreak area or had been there within 2 weeks of the interview.
source: About half of the interviews (21 of 40) were conducted with experts who were in the outbreak area (defined HZs affected by EVD or Goma, the site of the international response base) or had been there within 2 weeks of the interview.

claim: Four experts had never been in the outbreak area.
source: Four experts had never been in the outbreak area.

claim: Experts correctly identified Mabalako as the highest-risk health zone in December, attributing an average 82% probability of exceeding 2 cases.
source: Experts correctly identified Mabalako as the highest-risk HZ in December. They attributed an average 82% probability of exceeding 2 cases

claim: Mabalako reported 38 cases in December, exceeding all thresholds.
source: Mabalako reported 38 cases that month, exceeding all thresholds

claim: Mandima had no reported cases in December but was assigned a relatively high probability (72%) of exceeding two cases.
source: Interestingly, Mandima, which had no reported cases, was assigned a relatively high probability (72%) of exceeding two cases, indicating some overestimation in this zone.

claim: In January, Beni and Mabalako accounted for most cases (22 and 11, respectively).
source: In January, Beni and Mabalako again accounted for most cases (22 and 11, respectively)

claim: Experts underestimated the scale of the outbreak in Beni in January, assigning 0% probability to exceeding 20 cases despite this threshold being surpassed.
source: However, experts underestimated the scale of the outbreak in Beni, assigning 0% probability to exceeding 20 cases there, despite this threshold being surpassed.

claim: Only Beni reported confirmed cases in February (9 cases), exceeding the six-case threshold.
source: Of the 11 nominated HZs, only Beni reported confirmed cases in February (9), exceeding the six-case threshold.

claim: Experts collectively assigned a 70% probability to Beni exceeding the six-case threshold in February.
source: Experts collectively assigned a 70% probability to this event.

claim: No cases were reported in any health zone during March.
source: No cases were reported in any HZ during March.

claim: The overall scores of individual experts varied between 0 and 0.6 across the four thresholds.
source: The overall scores of individual experts varied between 0 and 0.6 across the four thresholds.

claim: Experts scored best at the highest threshold (20 cases) and worst for forecasts of the lowest threshold (2 cases).
source: Collectively, the experts scored best at the highest threshold (20 cases) and worst for forecasts of the lowest threshold (2 cases).

claim: The gravity model ranked best among all forecasts at the two-case threshold.
source: Overall, the gravity model ranked best among all forecasts at the two-case threshold.

claim: The adjacency model performed better than the experts overall for the two-case threshold.
source: The adjacency model also performed better than the experts overall for the two-case threshold.

claim: In March, both models performed particularly badly compared to the experts for all thresholds.
source: however in March, both models performed particularly badly compared to the experts for all thresholds.

claim: None of the experts performed consistently well relative to the others.
source: None of the experts performed consistently well relative to the others

claim: Experts systematically forecasted higher risk of the lowest threshold (≥2 cases) than was warranted.
source: We found that experts systematically forecasted higher risk of the lowest threshold (≥2 cases) than was warranted

claim: Experts tended to forecast lower risk of exceeding the highest threshold (≥20 cases) than was borne out across all health zones.
source: but tended to forecast lower risk of exceeding the highest threshold (≥20 cases) than was borne out across all HZs

claim: When calculated across all months, the bias towards over-predicting low thresholds was present in 12 of the 15 experts.
source: When calculated across all months, this bias was present in 12 of the 15 experts.

claim: The models did not show clear, consistent bias in either direction.
source: The models did not show clear, consistent bias in either direction.

claim: Experts nominated seven further health zones to forecast in December.
source: Experts nominated seven further HZs to forecast in December

claim: The only two health zones not included in the default list but exceeding two cases were Butembo and Katwa.
source: The only two HZs not included in the default list but exceeding two cases were Butembo and Katwa.

claim: The gravity model performed comparably to some experts when forecasting for December and February in predicting flare-ups.
source: When considering the Brier score (Figure 7), we found that the gravity model performed comparably to some experts when forecasting for December and February.
evidence: Data from the study results with reference to Figure 7

claim: The adjacency model performed worse than all the experts in every month except February when forecasting flare-ups.
source: The adjacency model performed worse than all the experts in every month except February.

claim: In every month, the ensemble of experts did better than the models when forecasting flare-ups.
source: In every month, the ensemble of experts did better than the models

claim: Including the models in the ensembles reduced performance when forecasting flare-ups.
source: and including the models in the ensembles reduced performance.

claim: An ensemble combining the forecasts of all experts performed similarly to the two models.
source: An ensemble combining the forecasts of all experts performed similarly to the two models.

claim: Experts showed stronger bias than models forecasting two-case threshold exceedance.
source: Experts showed stronger bias than models forecasting two-case threshold exceedance.

claim: Experts and models both performed better when predicting exceedance of higher thresholds.
source: Experts and models both performed better when predicting exceedance of higher thresholds.

claim: The models tended to be better at risk-ranking areas than experts.
source: The models also tended to be better at risk-ranking areas than experts.

claim: Both forecasting methods performed better when considering higher case thresholds.
source: We found that both methods performed better when considering higher case thresholds.

claim: The better performance at higher thresholds is likely due to a combination of bias in both forecast types towards under-prediction of cases and the fact that there were few instances where the higher thresholds were reached.
source: This is likely to be due to a combination of bias in both forecast types towards under-prediction of cases and the fact that there were few instances where the higher thresholds were reached.

claim: No individual expert outperformed the ensembles overall.
source: Although individual experts frequently outperformed ensembles in individual instances, no individual expert outperformed the ensembles overall.

claim: The models tended to perform similarly to the ensemble representing more consistent performance across all forecasts.
source: The models tended to perform similarly to the ensemble representing more consistent performance across all forecasts.

claim: Experts' bias towards over-predicting low thresholds may be interpreted as over-cautiousness regarding the potential for geographic spread of the virus but confidence that transmission could be contained quickly.
source: This may be interpreted as over-cautiousness from the experts regarding the potential for geographic spread of the virus but confidence that transmission could be contained quickly.

claim: This study is the first to record experts' assessment of geographical risk at a local level during an epidemic.
source: To our knowledge, our study is the first to record experts' assessment of geographical risk at a local level during an epidemic
evidence: Authors' claim about the novelty of their study

claim: This study is the first comparison of outbreak response experts' predictions to those of models in real time.
source: and the first comparison of outbreak response experts' predictions to those of models in real time.
evidence: Authors' claim about the novelty of their study

claim: The study only began in the closing phase of the epidemic due to the timing and logistics of setting up the questionnaire.
source: Due to the timing and logistics of setting up the questionnaire, the study only began in the closing phase of the epidemic

claim: The relative performance of experts and models may differ during different phases of the epidemic.
source: whereas the relative performance of experts and models may differ during different phases of the epidemic.

claim: The stage of the epidemic meant that there was a substantial trend towards 'negative' results (i.e. no threshold exceedance), which is likely to favour some forecasting methods over others.
source: The stage of the epidemic also meant that there was a substantial trend towards 'negative' results (i.e. no threshold exceedance), which is likely to favour some forecasting methods over others.

claim: Experts were not all interviewed on the same day, and interviews occurred several days before the beginning of the month they were forecasting.
source: Additionally, experts were not all interviewed on the same day, and interviews occurred several days before the beginning of the month they were forecasting.

claim: The information available differed both between experts and with the model, which was run considering data up to the first day of each month.
source: This means that the information available differed both between experts and with the model, which was run considering data up to the first day of each month.

claim: It is possible that some of the experts involved in the study had ingested results from the authors' model or other models being used at the time.
source: It is also possible that some of the experts involved in the study had ingested results from our model, which were available through our online dashboard, or other models being used at the time.

claim: Models remain useful in outbreak response because there was no individual expert that performed consistently better than the models.
source: Firstly, while the models performed similarly to the ensemble forecasts of the experts, there was no individual expert that performed consistently better than the models.

claim: Models are much more easily scaled and generalized, making them simple to deploy in new contexts and to adapt as epidemics grow.
source: Secondly, models are much more easily scaled and generalized, making them simple to deploy in new contexts and to adapt as epidemics grow.
evidence: Based on knowledge about the properties of models

claim: Expert interviews are time-consuming and often inconvenient, especially in the context of outbreak response activities.
source: Expert interviews are time-consuming and often inconvenient, especially in the context of outbreak response activities, which are characteristically fast paced.
evidence: Based on knowledge about the practical challenges of expert elicitation

claim: Models offer a more convenient route to a quantified insight, which performs comparably to the way groups of experts may think.
source: Models therefore offer a more convenient route to a quantified insight, which from our results performs comparably to the way groups of experts may think.

claim: The results support the use of models in outbreak response.
source: The results support the use of models in outbreak response
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the study results

claim: There could be value in combining expert opinion and modelled forecasts to support the response to future outbreaks.
source: There could be value in combining expert opinion and modelled forecasts to support the response to future outbreaks.

claim: The forecasts were motivated by an aim to inform site selection for a planned vaccine trial.
source: Alongside supporting situational awareness, these forecasts were motivated by an aim to inform site selection for a planned vaccine trial.

claim: The objective was to identify areas that had seen no cases yet and thus were not already being supported by vaccination and other interventions, but were at high risk of still becoming affected by the EVD outbreak.
source: The objective was to identify areas that had seen no cases yet and thus were not already being supported by vaccination and other interventions, but were at high risk of still becoming affected by the EVD outbreak, thus allowing estimation of efficacy (Watson-Jones et al., 2022).
evidence: Description of the study objective with citation to Watson-Jones et al., 2022

claim: The model performed better than the experts when considering the lowest threshold in 4 of the 5 months covered by the survey.
source: The model performed better than the experts when considering the lowest threshold in 4 of the 5 months covered by the survey

claim: The model performed marginally better when ranking health zones by risk of ongoing transmission.
source: The model also performed marginally better when ranking HZs by risk of ongoing transmission, indicating that use of a model may improve prioritization of HZs when attributing resources.

claim: The study results suggest that experts are better at predicting simple time series than geographic distribution of cases.
source: This may suggest that experts are better at predicting simple time series than geographic distribution of cases.
evidence: Speculation based on comparison with previous studies

claim: The study results provide insight into how models and expert opinion could be combined when tackling future epidemics.
source: and provide insight into how models and expert opinion could be combined when tackling future epidemics.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the study results
